newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia-Singapore bridge can boost ties-ministers.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia-Singapore bridge can boost ties-ministers.

text.p: A second road link between Malaysia and Singapore could be a catalyst to improve bilateral ties, battered by a row that began in March, ministers from both countries said on Thursday.

"Normally misunderstandings even happen in families," Malaysian Minister of Works Samy Vellu told reporters after the topping-up ceremony of the nearly US$1.0 billion bridge, which will be opened to traffic on January 2.
"This bridge will also act as a catalyst for bringing about more relationships between the people of Malaysia and Singapore."
Samy Vellu said the bridge would be officially opened by the prime ministers of both countries next year.
Singapore's National Development Minister Lim Hng Kiang told reporters: "This is a very important link both symbolically as well as concretely."
"The bridge will serve as a catalyst for greater trade and tourism and it will lead to greater development on both sides of the link."

A spat between the two neighbours began when Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew said in a court affidavit made public in March that Malaysia's Johor Baru state was notorious for shootings, muggings and car jackings.

That triggered a heated response from Malaysia, and while Lee twice apologised for the remarks, media and some politicians in the two countries continued to exchange barbs. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said it would take time for ties to improve.

On Wednesday, Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar told parliament that ties were slowly returning to normal and the city state was committed to building a long-term relationship based on mutual respect.
The new 1.9-kilometre (1.2-mile) bridge joins Gelang Patah in the southern Malaysian state of Johor and Tuas in western Singapore island.
Samy Vellu said the dual three-lane bridge was capable of carrying 200,000 vehicles per day, four times the capacity of the existing causeway, and would greatly reduce chronic traffic congestion.

The Malaysian portion of the bridge was built at 1.3 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$494 million) by United Engineers (M) Berhad, a unit of the Renong Group. The Singapore side was built by the Public Works Department at Singapore $600 million (US$408 million).
Regarding plans to rebuild the existing causeway, Samy Vellu said Malaysia's Foreign Ministry who would make a formal presentation to the Singapore side.
